edits.english: GEMARA: The Mishnah teaches: Or if the mufla of the court was not there, the court is exempt. From where do we derive this halakha? Rav Sheshet said, and likewise the Sage of the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: For what reason did the Sages of the Mishnah say: If the court issued a ruling with regard to a matter with which the Sadducees agree, the judges are exempt? It is due to the fact that judges of such a court are not considered fit to issue rulings, since it was incumbent upon them to learn that halakha that is written explicitly in the Torah, and they did not learn it. Similarly, in a case where the mufla of the court was not there, the judges are also exempt, as it was incumbent upon them to learn and they did not learn.

GEMARA. We learned in the Mishnah: Or if the mufla of the court was not there – the court is exempt. From where do we derive that this is the halakha? Rav Sheshet said, and likewise the Sage of the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: For what reason did the Sages say in the Mishnah: If the court issued a ruling with regard to a matter with which the Sadducees agree – the judges are exempt? It is because judges of such a court are not considered fit to issue rulings, since it was incumbent upon them to learn and they did not learn. Similarly, if the mufla of the court was not there, they are also exempt, because it was incumbent upon them to learn and they did not learn.

In the book Be'er Sheva, it wondered what this has to do with the mufla of the court. And in Ḥak Natan, it explains that just as in another place they should have learned and did not learn, so too here – they should have waited until the mufla of the court arrived and then ruled on this question.

We further learned in the Mishnah: “Assembly” is stated there and “assembly” is stated here… the court will not be liable unless all the judges will be fit to issue rulings. And the Gemara asks: And there, from where do we derive that all of them must be fit to issue rulings? And the Gemara answers: This is as Rav Ḥisda says that the verse states concerning the appointment of the seventy Elders by Moses: “That they may stand there with you” (Numbers 11:16), to say that “with you” means: Similar to you, Moses, in the sense that they must all be fit to issue rulings.
And there, from where do we derive it? - that all of them must be fit to issue rulings.

edits.hebrew: אמר רב חסדא - גמר ממשה; דמשה אוקי סנהדרין דהוו כולן ראויין להוראה, דכתיב: והתיצבו שם עמך, עמך בדומין לך, דליהוי (הם) כולן ראויין להוראה. ה"נ בעינן דסנהדרי דעלמא ליהוו ראויין להוראה. והואיל ומצינו דעדה האמורה כאן כולן ראויין להוראה, שמעינן מינה נמי דהיינו סנהדרי גדולה, דתניא בת"כ: עדת ישראל עדה המיוחדת לכל ישראל, ואיזו זו — סנהדרי גדולה:

edits.english: Rav Ḥisda says - He derives it from Moses; for Moses established a Sanhedrin where all its members were fit to issue rulings, as it is written: “And they shall stand there with you,” meaning “with you” in the sense of “similar to you,” that they should all be fit to issue rulings. So too, we require that the Sanhedrin in general should be fit to issue rulings. And since we find that the “assembly” mentioned here refers to judges all of whom are fit to issue rulings, we also learn from it that this refers to the Great Sanhedrin, as it is taught in Torat Kohanim: “Assembly of Israel” refers to an assembly unique to all of Israel, and which is this? The Great Sanhedrin.

We further learned in the Mishnah: “Assembly” is stated there and “assembly” is stated here… unless all of them are fit to issue rulings. And they ask: And there, from where do we derive that all of them are fit to issue rulings? And they answer: This is as Rav Ḥisda says, the verse states concerning the appointment of the seventy Elders by Moses: “That they may stand there with you” (Numbers 11:16), meaning that “with you” refers to those similar to you, Moses, that they should all be fit to issue rulings.

And they ask: And say that “with you” means that they shall be fit for the Divine Presence, and the verse intends to say that they should stand together to receive the Divine Presence! Rather, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says: We learn that all of them must be fit to issue rulings from what the verse states concerning the judges whom Moses appointed: “And they shall judge the people at all times…and ease your burden from upon you and bear it with you” (Exodus 18:22), meaning that “with you” signifies: Similar to you.

edits.hebrew: ואימא עמך משום שכינה - דלגופיה הוא דאתא, כלומר: שיהו עומדין עמך ולא יכנסו לפני ולפנים במקום שכינה, דסלקא דעתא אמינא: והואיל דכתב אספה לי, דיכנסו במקום שכינה. קא משמע לן [לשון אחר]: עמך משום שכינה, כלומר: ברור צדיקים גמורים שאני רוצה להשרות שכינה עליהם:

edits.english: And say that “with you” is for the Divine Presence - for it came for its own sake, meaning: that they should stand with you and not enter before the innermost part, in the place of the Divine Presence. For one might have thought, since it is written “Gather for Me,” that they should enter the place of the Divine Presence. This comes to teach us. [Another explanation]: “With you” is for the Divine Presence, meaning: choose perfectly righteous people upon whom I wish to cause My Divine Presence to rest.
With you, similar to you - that they should be fit to issue rulings.

And they ask: And say that “with you” means for the Divine Presence, and the verse intends to say that they should stand together to receive the Divine Presence! Rather, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says: We learn that all of them must be fit to issue rulings from what the verse states concerning the judges whom Moses appointed: “And they shall judge the people at all times…and ease your burden from upon you and bear it with you” (Exodus 18:22), meaning that “with you” signifies: Similar to you.

Rashi explains in one interpretation – for the sake of the Divine Presence, that they must be great men worthy for the Divine Presence to rest upon them. And in another explanation, he wrote that it comes to say that they should be with him, but not right next to him, because Moses entered the holy place to receive his prophecy, and they are forbidden to do so. And the Rosh wrote, for the sake of the Divine Presence – that they should be with him so that the Divine Presence may rest upon them.
